description: North coast east of Havana: beaches and the odd break when winter swell pushes in. The Bahamas block a lot of Atlantic swell; when it gets through you get waves. Varadero’s the resort strip; the surf’s fickle and the scene’s small.

name: Provincia de Guantánamo
description: Eastern tip: Baracoa and Yumuri. Yumuri’s the wave that gets the hype, a pebbled rivermouth point and the best-known break in Cuba. September to December for consistency. Rugged, green, and a long way from Havana; the surf’s the draw for the few who make it.

name: Provincia de Holguín
description: North coast: Gibara and the coast that faces the Atlantic. Short, punchy waves when swell and wind align; winter’s the window. Uncrowded and underdeveloped for surf; you’re exploring as much as scoring.

name: Provincia de Pinar del Río
description: Western province: the end of the island and north coast exposure. A few breaks when Atlantic swell wraps in; winter best. Tobacco and countryside; the surf’s not the main draw but the coast gets waves when the charts say so.

name: Curaçao
description: Spanish Waters is the windsurf and SUP hub; Playa Kanoa does kite. Klein Curaçao, an hour and a half by boat, has the best waves in the ABCs when you get there. The island’s wind and flat water more than reef; bring a board or rent from Surfspot Curaçao.

name: San Pedro
description: District on the island’s west side: quieter than Willemstad and the main lagoon. Some coast for kite and windsurf when the trades blow; the surf’s not the draw. Base for a relaxed stay with water access.

name: Santa Catharina
description: Bandariba district on the east: Santa Catharina bay and the coast that faces the wind. Kitesurfing’s the main activity; part of the area is private. About 20 minutes from Willemstad, and quieter than Spanish Waters.

name: Saint Andrew
description: North-east coast parish: Calibishie, Woodford Hill, Londonderry and Pagua Bay get Atlantic swell when it pushes in. Currents and undertows are serious; ask locals before paddling out. A small scene, and the island’s more about nature than surf.

name: Provincia de Barahona
description: South-west: the Pearl of the South and a surf stop on the Caribbean coast. Barranca reef and point when SE swell and NW wind align; autumn best. San Rafael and other beaches; the region’s raw and less built than the north.

name: Provincia de La Altagracia
description: Punta Cana and Bávaro: Macao is the surf beach, several peaks and room for all levels. October to March best; the rest of the coast is resort strip. Uvero Alto has waves and hotels. Not Cabarete, but surfable when you’re on the east.

name: Provincia de Peravia
description: South coast around Bani: a few breaks when Caribbean swell and wind line up. Quieter than the north coast; the province is sugar and coast, not the main surf trail. Autumn for the best of it.

name: Provincia de San Cristóbal
description: Inland and near the capital: no main surf coast. The province borders Santo Domingo; surfers head north to Cabarete or east to Macao. The hub between south and north.

name: Provincia de Santo Domingo
description: Capital province: La Boya is the break near the city, intermediate up, busy on weekends. Most surf traffic goes north to Encuentro and Cabarete. The airport’s here; the waves are elsewhere.

name: Puerto Plata
description: Cabarete and Encuentro sit here: the main surf zone in the country. Encuentro has Destroyers, Coco Pipe, the Main Break and Bobo’s; October to April best. Puerto Plata airport under 30 minutes. The north coast’s wave hub.

name: Samaná
description: The peninsula: Las Galeras, Rincón and the bays. Beaches and snorkel first; when Atlantic swell gets in there’s the odd wave. Whales in the bay January to April. Quieter than Cabarete; you’re here for the coast and the vibe.

name: Departamento de La Libertad
description: La Libertad town and the coast that holds Punta Roca: the right-hand point that put the country on the map. El Sunzal and the rest of the corridor; March and April for dry season and clean waves. The port’s the hub; keep a low profile and your gear close.

name: Departamento de La Paz
description: The inside section of Punta Roca: the softer, more forgiving end of the same point. A few hundred yards from the main peak; when the main break’s too much, the crew shifts here. Same south swell, same warm water.

name: Departamento de La Unión
description: Far east: the Gulf of Fonseca and the coast that gets the tail of south swell. Less developed than La Libertad; when the wet season pushes in there’s surf. The east is quieter and more exploratory.

name: Departamento de San Miguel
description: Las Flores and El Cuco: rocky points and a long black-sand beach on the eastern stretch. Right-handers and a fishing-village vibe; the wet season’s when the swell’s on. Fewer crowds than the central coast.

name: Departamento de Sonsonate
description: West coast: Mizata and Los Cóbanos. Mizata’s the one with the waves and the space; Los Cóbanos is the fishing village. Same south swell as the rest of the country; less traffic than La Libertad.

name: Departamento de Usulután
description: Punta Mango and the east: the break that stayed under the radar until recently. Right-hand point and the kind of trip that involves a bit of mission. Wet season swell; the department’s for surfers who want to get away from the main strip.

name: Saint George
description: Parish that holds the capital, St George’s, and the south-west coast. SurfinGrenada runs lessons and charters; the island’s not a heavy surf destination but there are waves when the Atlantic sends swell. More kite and boat traffic than lineup.

name: Guadeloupe
description: Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre: Bois Jolan lagoon for kite, Le Moule for surf (Damencourt and La Bouelle). Trades December to June; the island’s wind and flat water first, then reef when the north swell hits.

name: L'Autre Bord
description: Stretch of the coast that gets the trades; kite and windsurf when the breeze is up. Part of the island’s wind corridor; the lagoon and reef options depend on the spot.

name: Le Helleux
description: Coastal zone with access to the same trade winds and lagoons as the rest of Grande-Terre. Kite and windsurf country; flat water when it’s on.

name: Les Galbas
description: Part of the south or east coast wind belt; shallow water and lagoon when the spot’s right. Trades December to June; rig where the breeze is clean.

name: Morel
description: Coastal area on the wind corridor; kite and windsurf when the easterlies blow. Same season as the rest of the island; flat or choppy depending on the spot.

name: Rodrigue
description: Section of the coast that faces the trades; lagoon or reef depending on the exact spot. December to June for wind; bring your own gear or hook up with a local school.

name: Zamy
description: Coastal zone with trade-wind exposure; kite and windsurf when the spot works. Part of the same wind season as the rest of Guadeloupe.

name: Departamento de Escuintla
description: El Paredón and Sipacate: black sand, Pacific swell, and the spot that put Guatemala on the surf map. Beach breaks and a growing scene; November best. About two and a half hours from the capital; Swell and the surf camps are here.

name: Departamento de Jutiapa
description: South-east: a sliver of Pacific coast. La Barrona and the beaches get swell when it pushes in; not the main surf corridor. November to April; the department’s more inland than coastal.

name: Departamento de Retalhuleu
description: Pacific coast: Champerico and the strip toward the Mexican border. Beach breaks when the wet season swell’s on; May to November. Less developed than Escuintla; the coast’s raw.

name: Departamento de San Marcos
description: Tilapa and Tilapita: the twin beaches on the Pacific, black sand and fewer crowds. Maya Jade Surf and the national team train here. Wet season for waves; the coast’s low-key compared to El Paredón.

name: Departamento de Santa Rosa
description: Pacific strip: Monterrico and Las Lisas. Black sand, beach breaks, and the same wet-season swell as the rest of the coast. Turtle nesting and mangrove; the surf’s part of the draw, not the only one.

name: Suchitepequez Department
description: Pacific coast: Iztapa and the river-mouth breaks between the jetties. Lefts and rights; medium to high tide, SE to SW swell. Thirty minutes from Puerto San José; the department’s on the main surf corridor.

name: Sud
description: South department: Jacmel and the coast east of it. Ti Mouillage for beginners, Kabic for size, La Brésilienne when it’s serious. November to March for swell; the Haiti Surf Guesthouse and a handful of spots. Uncrowded and still emerging; infrastructure’s thin.

name: Kingston
description: The capital: the airport’s here and Bull Bay’s 10 minutes away. Jamnesia Surf Club and the Copa break are in the parish next door; Kingston’s the base for a surf trip, not the wave. Rent a board, get a transfer, and head east.

name: Portland
description: Boston Bay and the north-east: the parish that has Jamaica’s main surf beach. Consistent swell, jerk stands on the sand, and a scene that’s been there for years. November to May best; two hours from Kingston. The one to hit if you’re coming for waves.

name: Saint Andrew
description: Bull Bay and Copa: the heart of the island’s surf scene. Jamnesia Surf Club is here, Billy Wilmot and the national team. Lighthouse and the breaks east of Kingston; November to February when the winter swell hits. Ten minutes from the airport.

name: Saint Thomas
description: East end: the Makka Pro has run here, the first pro surf contest in the Caribbean. The break’s powerful and fast; experienced crew. The parish is the quiet end of the island; the wave’s the draw when the swell’s on.

name: Bonneville
description: Anse Bonneville: the Caravelle peninsula and the beach they call Plage des Surfeurs. Atlantic swell on the reef; November to March best. Surf schools and rentals; left side for the heavy stuff, right for beginners. La Trinité.

name: Hardy
description: Coastal stretch that gets the same Atlantic trade wind and swell as the rest of the island. Kite and surf when the spot works; November to June for wind. Part of the same corridor as Pointe Faula and the main lagoons.

name: Martinique
description: Pointe Faula for kite, Anse Michel and Cap Est for the lagoons, Anse Bonneville for surf. Trades November to June; the island’s wind and flat water first, then reef when the north swell hits. No wetsuit.

name: Baja California
description: Northern Baja: K38 is the right-hand point that San Diego surfers hit on the way south, rocky reef and long walls. Rosarito and Ensenada in between; fish tacos and cold cerveza when you’re done. Summer through winter for south swell; booties for the rocks and urchins. Forty-five minutes from the border.

name: Baja California Sur
description: Todos Santos is Mexico’s first World Surfing Reserve: San Miguel, Salsipuedes, Killers on the island when it’s big. Pueblo Mágico, galleries and good food; the wave that birthed Mexican surf culture is here. Cabo’s the resort strip; the real surf’s north. Winter NW swell; desert and ocean.

name: Chiapas
description: Short Pacific coast: Puerto Madero, Boca del Cielo, El Zapotal. Powerful beach breaks and the odd barrel; May to October when the south swell hits. Raw and uncrowded; the state’s jungle and highlands, the coast’s still under the radar. Paredon for the heavy stuff.

name: Colima
description: Pascuales is the one: black sand, expert-only barrels, and the comparison to Puerto Escondido is real. Winter for the best of it; NE offshores in the morning before it blows out. Muddy roads, mosquitoes in summer, and a scene that’s there for the wave. Colima’s cheap, heavy, and uncrowded.

name: Guerrero
description: Troncones and La Saladita: the mellow left point and the beach breaks north of Zihuatanejo. May to September for size; November to February for learners. Fish tacos and palapas; the coast’s low-rise and the lineup’s relaxed. Acapulco’s the big city; this is the surf strip.

name: Jalisco
description: Puerto Vallarta and the bay: Boca de Tomates for beginners and kite when the wind’s up. The Ameca River mouth, palapa ceviche, and the airport right there. Sayulita and the real waves are in Nayarit next door; Jalisco’s the gateway and the city break.

name: Michoacán
description: Playa Azul, La Ticla, Rio Nexpa: rivermouth points and beach breaks that peel. Summer’s the season; the coast’s cheap and the waves are consistent. Colima’s Pascuales is next door when you want heavy. Michoacán’s the green, low-key stretch between the big names.

name: Nayarit
description: Sayulita’s the name: the main beach for longboard and learner waves, Punta Mita and San Pancho when you want a bit more. Riviera Nayarit; an hour and a half from Puerto Vallarta. Summer for size, winter for smaller and cleaner. Crowded when it’s good; the town’s built around surf and tacos.

name: Oaxaca
description: Puerto Escondido and Zicatela: the Mexican Pipeline. Heavy, barreling beach break; La Punta’s mellower, the main peak’s for experts. April to October it gets huge; dry season’s cleaner and smaller. Oaxaca’s food and mezcal; the town’s bohemian and the lineup’s serious. One of the world’s best waves.

name: Quintana Roo
description: Caribbean side: Cancún, Playa del Carmen, Cozumel. Playa Chac Mool and Delfines get windswell when the nortes blow; November to April. One to three feet, beginner waves and kite. You’re here for the reef and the resorts; the surf’s a bonus, not the reason.

name: Sinaloa
description: Mazatlán’s the hub: Playa Bruja, Los Pinos, Stone Island. Pacific swell and warm water; the malecón and the shrimp. San Blas and the coast north when you want to get away. Sinaloa’s the state the headlines know; the coast’s surf, ceviche, and a scene that’s been there for years.

name: Tamaulipas
description: Gulf coast: Tampico, Los Americanos. Short fetch and windswell; two to four foot when the wind and swell align. Not the Pacific; you’re chasing the odd clean day. Warm water, a small local scene, and the kind of surf trip that’s about the coast as much as the wave.

name: Veracruz
description: Veracruz city and the central Gulf: El Chachalaco, Destapador, Marti. Windswell when the nortes push in; the state’s coffee and jarocho culture. Not a premier surf destination; when the swell hits the local crew’s out. Boca del Río and the malecón; the surf’s part of the mix.

name: Departamento de Carazo
description: Rocky shelves at La Boquita and the reef at Casares turn small Pacific swell into wedgy peaks, waist to head-high with punch when it lines up. Tides and cobbles matter; most locals surf it mid to high and wear booties when it is bigger. Close enough to Managua and Masaya for a day strike, but the road, currents, and shorebreak make it better for confident intermediates and up.

name: Departamento de Chinandega
description: Heavier beachbreak defines this northwest corner, with El Boom near Jiquilillo famous for thick, hollow peaks that do not need much swell. Consistent offshore winds and sandbanks mean barrels when the sand is right, but you are far from big towns and it is mostly intermediate to expert territory. Access is part of the adventure here: bumpy tracks, small fishing villages, and long, hot paddles in and out.

name: Departamento de León
description: Black-sand points and rivermouths here can run for hundreds of meters when the sand is groomed and the offshore trades are whistling. El Transito offers a friendlier setup with several peaks and a mellow town vibe, while Puerto Sandino turns on for long, fast walls when the swell gets serious. It is classic Nicaragua: consistent offshores, strong currents, and more power than first-timers expect.

name: Departamento de Managua
description: West of the capital, beaches like Pochomil and Masachapa pick up the same Pacific energy but in a slightly softer, more forgiving package. These are the breaks Managuans hit for weekend sessions, with shifting sandbars, rips, and afternoon onshores that reward early starts. Not as famous as Rivas or León, but you can still score fun peaks without the surf-camp crowds.

name: Departamento de Rivas
description: Sand-bottom points and reefs from Popoyo down toward San Juan del Sur are why surfers keep flying to Nicaragua. Popoyo and nearby breaks offer everything from playful peelers to heavy reefs when the swell jumps, while the lake-fed offshores can keep the faces groomed for hours. It is busier every year, with boat shuttles, surf resorts, and party towns, but you still find quieter corners if you are willing to explore and walk.

name: Chiriquí Province
description: Long, straight Las Lajas is the obvious draw here, a wide sandbar that turns west swells into running peaks and playful walls. Farther offshore, island setups like Morro Negrito focus that same energy into punchier, more technical waves for intermediate and advanced surfers on surf-camp programs. The province still feels agricultural and sleepy compared to the capital, so you trade nightlife for empty lineups and sunsets over mangroves and rice fields.

name: Panamá Oeste
description: This stretch just west of the Canal is where Panama City surfers sneak out for quick sessions, with beachbreaks around Punta Chame and Malibu offering fun walls when the tide and wind cooperate. On small days it is mellow enough for learners; when a solid south swell hits, rips and closeouts make it more serious. Easy access and weekend crowds are the tax you pay for being this close to the city.

name: Panamá Province
description: City life meets surf here, with Panama City’s skyline only a drive from Pacific beaches like Veracruz and the more exposed stretches east of the Canal. These waves are not as consistently clean as the Azuero or Veraguas points, but they light up under seasonal south swells and are the first choice for a dawn patrol before work. Expect urban traffic, mixed sand quality, and changing water clarity alongside the convenience of big-city restaurants and nightlife when you come in.

name: Provincia de Bocas del Toro
description: Caribbean reefs around Isla Colón and Bastimentos have put this province on the global surf map, from long lefts at Carenero Point to heavier barrels at Bluff and Paunch when a solid north swell hits. December through March is the prime window, with warm water, boat taxis instead of carparks, and jungle backdrops right down to the high-tide line. Swell is more fickle than the Pacific and crowds spike quickly, but the mix of island life and reef setups keeps people coming back.

name: Provincia de Coclé
description: The “Riviera Pacífica” resorts sit on beachbreaks like El Palmar and Río Mar, where south swells wrap into rideable peaks for everyone from learners to intermediates. On the better days, the outer reefs and rivermouths nearby offer punchier sections while still staying user-friendly compared to the heavier points farther west. It is an easy, family-friendly base: paved access, condos and golf courses, and restaurant-lined beaches instead of pure wilderness.

name: Provincia de Colón
description: Hidden Caribbean coves and reef set-ups around Portobelo and Nombre de Dios turn short-period trade-wind swell into surprisingly fun waves when the timing is right. It is a place for patient surfers who do not mind boat rides, patchy forecasts, and the odd day of flat turquoise water between windows. The trade-off is warm, clear water, jungle-clad headlands, and hardly any surf infrastructure once you leave the highway.

name: Provincia de Los Santos
description: Down on the Azuero Peninsula, Playa Venao has become Panama’s best-known beachbreak, a horseshoe bay that serves up rippable peaks from chest-high runners to overhead walls. A short drive away, Cambutal adds heavier, more powerful waves when the swell jumps, with black-sand beaches and nearby points that suit confident intermediates and up. This coast now mixes boutique hotels and hostels with cattle country, so you get a real mix of surfers, fishermen, and long-time locals in town.

name: Provincia de Veraguas
description: Santa Catalina is the headline here, a powerful right that reels along the reef and can hold serious size while still offering shoulders for confident intermediates. Morrillo and other nearby beaches spread out the swell with punchy peaks and plenty of room to move when the swell direction is right. The province feels remote once you leave Santiago: long drives, simple fishing villages, and few backup options if the swell or wind do not cooperate, but that is exactly why many surfers love it.

name: Provincia del Darién
description: Way out toward the Colombian border, this is one of Central America’s wildest coasts, with mangroves, river mouths, and unexplored Pacific points that see more fishermen than surfers. Getting to any wave here means serious logistics, permits, and local knowledge, plus an eye on security and weather. It is not a casual surf destination, but for expedition-minded crews, the idea of empty, unknown setups hidden in rainforest is the whole appeal.

name: Aguada
description: West of the more famous clusters, reef and cobble pockets along the highway pick up the same winter north and northwest pulses, with beach setups that favor mid to high tide when the trades stay light. Guanabano and Charco side breaks turn small to medium swell into fun walls, but rocks, shorebreak, and longshore currents keep it more of a locals and road trip scene than a resort strip.

name: Aguadilla
description: Crash Boat’s pier and turquoise bay are the postcard, but the wave is a shifting sand and reef mix that can throw punchy lefts and rights when a solid north swell hits. Surfer’s and Punta Borinquen add heavier options nearby, while Wilderness stays expert territory with currents and remote access. Mornings beat the west wind; weekends pack the sand and the parking lot fills fast.

name: Arecibo
description: La Marginal runs along the waterfront as a serious reef wave when the Atlantic is awake, with long walls that have hosted high level contests and plenty of hungry locals on good days. Caza y Pesca offers a softer, sandier contrast for smaller days and learners when the ocean settles. Expect classic north coast seasonality: bigger, rawer surf October through March, and more wind chop when the trades crank.

name: Canóvanas Municipio
description: Rainforest slopes and shopping corridors define the interior here, so you will not walk straight from a town plaza to a lineup. Surfers treat it as a base for quick runs to the northeast highway beaches, where the same north swell trains that light up the whole north shore are a short drive away. Trade off is traffic and weekend crowds near the malls, but you sleep cooler in the hills than on the sand.

name: Carolina Municipio
description: Metro east coast energy shows up as consistent sandbars along the long city beaches, where northwest and north swells wrap into rideable peaks within minutes of the airport hotels. Rips run real when it gets overhead, and the urban backdrop means crowds, street parking games, and the usual city runoff after rain. Dawn patrol is the move if you want cleaner faces before the sea breeze builds.

name: Culebra
description: Flamenco frames the island’s most famous crescent, where small to medium Caribbean swell can peel across an outside reef with longboard friendly shoulders when the period lines up. Getting boards and bodies here means ferries or flights, higher costs, and planning around weather windows that can go flat for days. Reward is thin crowds in the water compared with the main island and water so clear you will watch the bottom between sets.

name: Dorado
description: Resort beaches and reef ledges along this stretch turn on when winter north swells push down the Atlantic side of the island. Kikita style setups favor surfers who know the rock entries and tide stages, while inside sections stay softer for mixed groups on smaller days. It is an easy day trip from San Juan, which keeps the lineups educated and competitive on the best swells.

name: Fajardo Municipio
description: The headlands here face open Atlantic blue, but many public coves sit behind reef shelves that trim size and favor snorkeling and boat days. When a strong north swell wraps, you hunt exposed corners and outside reefs while managing steady trade wind texture on the face. It is less of a single famous beachbreak and more of a conditions game compared with the sandbar strips farther west along the same coast.

name: Luquillo Municipio
description: La Pared is the reliable beginner to intermediate sandbar, busy because it breaks often and sits right off the main road. La Selva is the darker twin, a longer walk to a heavier reef that thins the crowd but demands respect for shallow coral and local priority. Northeast exposure means classic winter north swell season, afternoon trades, and powerful rips whenever the surf gets serious.

name: Manatí Municipio
description: Long Atlantic beaches west of the capital pick up the same winter pulses as the rest of the north shore, with Tortuguero offering open sand where bigger days stack and move water fast. Mar Chiquita is the dramatic pool inside a rock horseshoe, photogenic and occasionally surfable on the outer surge, but it is not a daily lineup spot. Expect roadside parking scrambles, weekend families, and the usual north coast urchins and rocks when you chase reefs.

name: Municipio de Isabela
description: Jobos is the social hub, splitting a mellow inside sand section from a reef that turns on for intermediate and advanced riders when the banks line up. Middles and Shacks step up the commitment with hollower reef energy and heavier hold downs on the best swells. Northwest exposure makes it one of the island’s busiest winter arenas, so patience and etiquette matter as much as paddle fitness.

name: Patillas Municipio
description: Southeast facing pockets like Inches turn short period energy into small, playful faces that suit longboards and learners when the Caribbean side wakes up. Reefs are shallow and the surf zone is compact, so a handful of surfers can feel crowded fast. It is a quieter corner of the island for better or worse, with longer drives back to surf shops and ding repair if you snap a fin on the rock.

name: Quebradillas Municipio
description: Guajataca sits under tall limestone cliffs with rivermouth influence and heavy water when the Atlantic is angry, a raw beachbreak and reef mix that demands respect for currents and closeouts. The old tunnel overlook is part of the vibe, but there are no lifeguards and few frills, so you pack water and watch the rips. Best on cleaner winter swells; summer can look pretty and still be unrideable chop.

name: Rincón Municipio
description: Domes and Indicators are the postcard points, drawing long, groomed faces when winter norths line up with the offshore flow. María’s and Tres Palmas step into serious reef territory on bigger swells, where thick Hawaiian style energy reminds you this coast is not all longboard peelers. The town is built around surf tourism, so expect packed lineups, rental traffic, and plenty of eyes on every set.

name: San Juan
description: City sandbars from Ocean Park to Condado turn on for quick sessions between meetings when a north swell hits, with La Ocho offering a known reef peak for those who understand the slab and the crowd. Wind, urban runoff after rain, and swimmers inside make it a heads up zone compared with open country breaks. You trade raw ocean solitude for walkability, food, and nightlife one block from the wax.

name: Vega Alta
description: Tocones and the Cerro Gordo headland area focus north swell into sand and reef peaks along a less built up strip of the metro west coast. Winter is the reliable season; summer can go small and windy fast. Parking and security vary by pull off, so pack light, hide valuables, and surf with a buddy when the surf gets bigger and the rips widen.

name: Vega Baja
description: Puerto Nuevo’s limestone wall shelters a postcard pool while Los Tubos handles winter juice on the outer bars with fast, hollow sections for riders who know the lineup. The same north coast crowds and currents apply, with weekend traffic and families sharing the sand beside serious swell. It is classic Atlantic Puerto Rico, beautiful and powerful when the ocean decides to turn on.

name: Quartier de Lorient
description: Reef fingers off the sand split swell into a few separate peaks, so on clean days you can pick a softer shoulder or a steeper wall without leaving the bay. The leeward side of the island keeps many beaches flat, which makes this one of the more reliable learner to intermediate corners when a northeast pulse lines up with southeast offshore flow. It still needs real swell to work, and urchins plus shallow coral mean booties and tide awareness are standard.

name: Toiny
description: Atlantic swell marches in here with little to soften it first, so the beach can turn fast, heavy, and close to shore when the period stacks up. This is the serious side of the island, with steady wind texture and currents that keep casual swimmers away from the water. Pack experience, patience for shifting banks, and respect for a small crew who treat the place like a specialty wave rather than a beach day.

name: Cupecoy
description: Limestone walls hide a narrow cove where a right reef can light up on the right northwest angle, though flat spells are common and you are always negotiating rips. Access is down steps from cliff top parking, and the far end carries a clothing optional vibe that changes the beach culture from family strips elsewhere on the island. Winter into spring tends to offer the better windows; when it is tiny, the cliffs still make it a scenic swim or snorkel spot.

name: Mullet Bay
description: South coast sand stretches between the airport buzz and the resort clusters, with beachbreak peaks that favor loggers and funboards when a southwest swell couples with offshore flow from the northeast. It is one of the easier corners to read from shore, but shifting sand, jet blast noise, and weekend beach traffic remind you this is still a busy holiday island. Early sessions beat the onshore sea breeze that often builds through the afternoon.

name: Saint Lucia
description: The island sits outside the main North Atlantic track, so surf days are real but selective, with northeast reef setups like Pigeon Point offering one of the more consistent reef peaks when a solid trade swell wraps in. Soufriere’s dramatic bays look made for postcards; a few reefs can turn on for intermediates when conditions align, but many days are better for diving and boat trips than boards. Expect warm water year round, sharp coral in the lineup, and quiet lineups whenever the charts go flat.

name: Parish of Charlotte
description: Windward exposure along this east coast means raw Atlantic energy, with rivermouth and bay setups near places like Biabou and Georgetown turning on when long period swell meets the right sand. It is the island’s longer, rougher shoreline, so access can be rugged, roads twist, and rips run honest on bigger days. When it is on, you trade convenience for empty peaks; when it is off, you are mostly looking at wind chop and shorebreak watching.

name: Parish of Saint George
description: Sheltered bays around Calliaqua hide a reef left at Blue Lagoon that can peel on southeast to northeast energy, with a slanted reef entry that punishes lazy footwork. Marina traffic and yachts share the water, so etiquette around boats and dinghies matters as much as the wave itself. It is rarely a crowded marquee break, but urchins, sharp rock, and occasional junk swell keep it firmly in the thinking surfer category.

name: Villa
description: Outside the reef, Villa Reef can offer a defined peak where longer period swell bends in across the Caribbean side, while the inner beach stays gentle enough for swimming most days. Hotels and villas crowd the narrow strip, so parking and lineup politics follow peak tourist weeks. Think mellow angles more often than power, with coral underfoot whenever it actually breaks.

name: Crown Point
description: The southwest corner stacks Caribbean swell against reef shelves near the airport headland, with a named reef setup at Crown Point that can peel when north to northeast energy lines up. Just around the cape, Pigeon Point adds a more exposed beachbreak mood with shifting sand and rocks underfoot. Flights, taxis, and day trippers keep the roads busy, but water stays warm and crowds in the surf stay modest compared with the beach bars onshore.

name: Sangre Grande
description: The town itself sits inland, but this northeast region is the gateway to Trinidad’s best Atlantic exposure, from Salybia and Sans Souci style setups to longer runs toward Toco when charts light up. Roads are slow, coconut coast drives, and most surfers plan full day missions rather than a lunch hour session. When a solid north swell fires, the reward is powerful sand and reef waves and a small island scene that still feels far from Port of Spain.

name: Tobago
description: Mount Irvine’s right reef has been the island’s headline session since the early days, with long walls when the Caribbean side wakes up and enough size to separate confident riders from learners. The north coast adds heavier reef options when winter groundswell wraps, while the leeward southwest stays friendlier for mixed groups on smaller days. Tobago trades big city infrastructure for village pace, so board repair, spare leashes, and patience with ferry weather are part of the trip.

name: Cruz Bay
description: The main ferry dock and town beach sit inside a busy bay, so boards here mean dodging moorings, swimmers, and afternoon traffic from Red Hook boats. When a solid north swell runs, locals look to tucked pockets like Turner Bay or the more exposed reef setups off the south shore trail beaches, not the harbor sand. Plan on renting a jeep or hiking for cleaner peaks, and expect national park rules, parking limits, and crowds whenever the forecast turns green.

name: Saint Croix Island
description: The north shore picks up winter north swell better than the leeward towns, with Judith's Fancy offering a known reef peak that locals guard on small to medium days. Cane Bay steals the postcards for diving, yet it can throw rideable walls when angle and period align, just remember urchins, trade wind texture, and shallow reef. The island is quieter than St Thomas, but you still fly boards in and hope rental cars survive the steep roads.

name: Saint John Island
description: Two thirds of the land is national park, which keeps coastlines gorgeous and access sometimes a hike from Cruz Bay. Cinnamon turns into the island’s most surfed sand and reef mix when winter norths fill in, with waist to chest runners that suit loggers and intermediates more than chargers. Parking, trailheads, and day trip boats from St Thomas can thin the water or pack it overnight, depending on the week.

name: Saint Thomas Island
description: Hull Bay on the north side is the name locals quote first, a reef break that wakes up on north swell with south to southeast offshore flow when the weather pattern cooperates. Sapphire and the east end resorts see more wind and jet skis than pure surf, though an angled swell can still peel across outside reefs. Steep roads, cruise ship days in Charlotte Amalie, and limited board shops mean you pack spare gear and surf early before the trades chop the faces.

name: Alabama
description: Gulf sandbars from Orange Beach westward turn windswell and the occasional hurricane swell into waist to overhead peaks when the Gulf actually moves. It is not California consistency, but long jetties, pier shadows, and summer crowds are the trade for warm water and mellow local scenes between flat spells.

name: Alaska
description: Cold North Pacific energy lights up remote points and beachbreaks from the Panhandle to the Aleutian arc, with Yakutat Bay and nearby setups famous for heavy water sessions when long period lows track north. Kodiak and southcentral coves add more options, but you are always balancing short daylight, wildlife, rock bottom, and serious logistics compared with a road trip in the Lower 48.

name: California
description: More than a thousand miles of Pacific frontage pack everything from thick winter northwest reefs to mellow summer points along the south coast. Names like Steamer Lane and Lower Trestles get the headlines, yet everyday reality is fog, currents, crowded urban peaks, and marine layer wind that rewards dawn patrols and local knowledge over guidebook bravado.

name: Delaware
description: A short Atlantic frontage relies on northeast groundswell and windswell wrapping into Delaware Bay mouths and jettied beaches, with Indian River Inlet one of the better known reef and sand mixes on a good day. Summers are often small and crowded with holiday beach traffic, while the best windows follow offshore storms when water stays cold and rips run honest.

name: Florida
description: Two different surf lives sit here: Atlantic beachbreaks and reefs from Amelia Island through the Space Coast and South Beach, and Gulf side wind chop and hurricane swells along the Panhandle and west coast. New Smyrna Inlet and the Cocoa stretch see year round traffic, while the Gulf needs tropical systems to wake up. Expect sharks, jet skis, and packed lineups wherever the sandbars line up.

name: Georgia
description: Barrier islands face the open Atlantic with Tybee and Jekyll offering approachable sand peaks when a northeast or east swell couples with west wind. It is a smaller, fickle scene than the Carolinas to the north, with summer mush, spring tidal swings, and more longboard days than heavy reef sessions.

name: Hawaii
description: Open Pacific swell trains slam north facing shores across the chain, from long period winter giants on Oahu’s North Shore to softer trade swell wraps on south and east exposures elsewhere. Pipeline and Honolua Bay are global references, but reef etiquette, local hierarchy, and shallow coral keep the bar high for visitors who fly in with fresh boards and big expectations.

name: Illinois
description: Surf here means freshwater Great Lakes, with Montrose and nearby Chicago breaks turning on when autumn lows stack fetch across Lake Michigan. Spring and summer can go flat for weeks, while winter sessions bring hoods, ice beards, and wind chill that separate committed locals from tourists. Access and water quality swing with urban runoff after storms.

name: Indiana
description: The state's surfable window is almost entirely the south end of Lake Michigan, where Michigan City and the Indiana Dunes picks up the same fall and winter lows as Chicago to the west. Wind direction matters more than ocean swell, so sideshore chop is common and the best days are often cold, gusty, and uncrowded for the wrong reasons.

name: Louisiana
description: Gulf marshes and muddy nearshore water hide a few beachbreaks and jetties that fire on hurricane swell, with Grand Isle the best known stretch when a storm tracks right. Most of the year is small wind chop or flat, plus summer heat, lightning risk, and occasional water quality issues after heavy rain.

name: Maine
description: Granite headlands and rivermouth sand create classic New England setups from Ogunquit’s river wave to scattered beach peaks up the coast. Winter north swells bring the size, but you earn it with cold water, snow on the beach, and weekend traffic from Boston when a good forecast leaks online.

name: Maryland
description: Assateague’s open ocean beaches and Ocean City’s jettied sandbars pick up Atlantic energy through fall and winter better than the protected Chesapeake shore. Summers skew weak and tourist heavy, while the best sessions line up with nor’easters and cold air that test your hood and your parking patience.

name: Massachusetts
description: Cape Cod points and outer beachbreaks turn on for New England groundswell, while Nahant’s Wall offers a heavier reef option near Boston when the angle fits. Nantucket Sound and inside bays stay mostly flat, so road miles add up fast and summer crowds fill the easy parking lots on the small days.

name: Michigan
description: No ocean means the Great Lakes are the stage, from Lake Superior reef setups near Marquette to booming Lake Michigan beachbreaks at Grand Haven when autumn gales stack. Forecast watching is everything, with offshore wind a rarity and the best waves often arriving when air and water are both frigid.

name: Minnesota
description: Lake Superior dominates the story, with Duluth’s Park Point and the St. Louis River mouth firing on the biggest wind events, while inland lakes stay flat. Ice and hypothermia are real hazards, so spring and fall shoulder seasons see the most boards in the water even when consistency is nothing like the coasts.

name: Mississippi
description: The Gulf Coast strip from Bay St. Louis east runs mostly windswell and the rare tropical swell, with pier and beachbreak peaks that favor longboards and patient locals. Water stays warm much of the year, but clarity and quality spike only when storms track favorably, otherwise it is ankle slappers and jet ski traffic.

name: New Hampshire
description: Only seventeen miles of Atlantic shore pack the state’s surf into Hampton and Rye style sandbars that need northeast swell and west wind to clean up. It is compact compared with Maine or Massachusetts, so crowds stack on good weekends and winter sessions mean thick rubber and rocky parking lots.

name: New Jersey
description: Sandy hook to Cape May lines up jetties, inlets, and summer beachbreaks that love a solid east or southeast pulse, with Manasquan Inlet one of the classic winter magnets when the North Atlantic wakes up. Water color and crowd density swing wildly, and summer onshore wind can turn a promising forecast into closeouts fast.

name: New York
description: Long Island’s south shore from Rockaway through Gilgo and the central beaches handles Atlantic groundswell, while Montauk points fire on the best fall and winter swells. Upstate is landlocked for surf, so the story is really downstate road trips, bridge tolls, and summer beach restrictions when the ocean goes small.

name: North Carolina
description: The Outer Banks funnel Atlantic energy into sand spits and pier peaks from Corolla to Cape Lookout, with Hatteras Island the spiritual center when a hurricane swell lights up beachbreaks for miles. Spring and summer can offer fun peaks too, but noreasters and named storms produce the memorable days that also bring rips, shorebreak rescues, and traffic on Highway 12.

name: Ohio
description: Lake Erie’s southern shore gives Cleveland’s Edgewater and Presque Isle near Erie their moments when strong winds blow up fetch long enough to build rideable chop and swell. It is not Hawaii, it is industrial skyline backdrops, zebra mussels, and sessions that last an hour before wind shifts ruin the surface.

name: Oregon
description: The whole Pacific Northwest playbook applies here, from long sandy beachbreaks at Pacific City and Cannon Beach to heavier reef setups farther north when winter lows track across the North Pacific. Winter swell windows can outlast the summer flat spells common farther south in California, but cold water, strong currents, and logging road access keep crowds thinner than the marketing photos suggest.

name: Pennsylvania
description: Surf means Lake Erie’s Presque Isle Bay mouth and similar Great Lakes setups when wind stacks water against the beaches at Erie. Inland valleys stay flat, so the community is small, seasonally driven, and used to driving a short distance for a short window when the map finally turns green.

name: Rhode Island
description: A tiny south facing Atlantic coast concentrates surf into Narragansett Bay entrances and reef points like Point Judith and Ruggles when southeast to east swell lines up with offshore flow from the west. Summer is often weak, while the standout sessions ride winter storms that also bring cold air and heavy rips along rocky shorelines.

name: South Carolina
description: Barrier islands from Cherry Grove through Folly pick up southeast swell and hurricane energy, with Charleston area sandbars offering playful peaks on the right tide. It is mellower than the Outer Banks to the north, with warm water, summer crowds, and afternoon sea breezes that can tear apart a promising morning forecast.

name: Texas
description: Gulf surfers live for hurricane season, when Padre Island and Corpus area sandbars turn on, while the rest of the year is windswell and patience. Crowds spike when a storm swell tracks into the Gulf, and shorebreak, stingrays, and long drives between cities are part of the package.

name: Virginia
description: Sandbridge and the Virginia Beach jetties handle Atlantic swell through fall and winter, with offshore islands and military airspace shaping access more than you would expect from a map. Summer is small and packed with beach tourism, while the better winter days reward thick wetsuits and early arrivals before the wind goes onshore.

name: Washington
description: Winter North Pacific groundswell marches into the Strait of Juan de Fuca and down the outer coast, with Westport Jetty and the Olympic Peninsula beaches the usual names when charts light up. Summer is often flat or blown out on the open coast, and logging roads, fog, and cold upwelling remind you this is not Southern California with pine trees.

name: Wisconsin
description: Lake Michigan dominates, with Sheboygan marketing itself as the Malibu of the Midwest when fall gales stack, and Milwaukee county beaches picking up similar windows closer to the city. Superior’s south shore adds heavier days near Ashland when conditions align, but ice out dates and bitter wind chills keep the calendar short for comfortable sessions.

name: Eastern District
description: Harbor villages along the drowned volcanic rim open onto south facing reef shelves where long period Southern Ocean energy wraps into fast, hollow sections on the right tide. Aunu'u sits just offshore with its own reef peaks and a short boat hop from the main island, while breaks near Faganeanea and the Pago corridor see regular traffic from locals and visiting military. Southeast trades build fast after breakfast, so dawn glass is currency, and shallow coral plus strong respect for village access rules come with every session.

name: Western District
description: The west end turns more toward the open Pacific, with Poloa and Amanave Bay among the heavier reef arenas when northwest or west swells line up through the islands. Sliding Rock and similar lava front setups can light up on specific angles but stay fickle, rippy, and sharp underfoot. Airport and highway sprawl around Tafuna make logistics easier than the east for fly ins, yet tsunami history and thin inside water mean you read the tide and treat every bigger set with caution.

name: New South Wales
description: Two thousand kilometres of Pacific-facing coast pack everything from city sandbars to long points and heavy reef slabs. The Pass at Byron and the northern Sydney stretch are global reference points, yet everyday surfing here is traffic, parking wars, summer onshores, and packed peaks whenever an east coast low fires. Champions and underground locals alike grew up in these beachbreaks, which makes etiquette and paddle fitness as important as the forecast.

name: Norfolk Island
description: Volcanic reef shelves ring this tiny outpost halfway to New Caledonia, with Slaughter Bay near Kingston offering one of the more consistent reef setups when southerly groundswell meets offshore northerly flow. Bumboras adds a punchier local option when banks line up, while cliff access bays stay empty for hikers willing to carry boards. You fly gear in, hope for spare wax, and lean on locals because there is no real surf retail scene when a bag goes missing.

name: Northern Territory
description: Tropical humidity and crocodile country frame a surf scene that is real but narrow compared with the southern capitals. Darwin area reefs and beachbreaks need specific swell windows and careful shark and croc awareness that most traveling surfers underestimate. When it connects you get warm, empty lineups; when it does not you are better off with a fishing rod than a fresh stick.

name: Queensland
description: Coral Sea energy lights up the points from the Sunshine Coast to the Gold Coast, where Snapper Rocks and the Superbank have hosted generations of CT talent and backyard pros. North of the border, trade wind summers and cyclone summers define two different games, with crowds, jet skis, and hungry locals on every good sandbank. It is Australia's most photographed surf strip, which is both the draw and the headache.

name: South Australia
description: Southern Ocean lows march into the Bight and wrap along the Mid and Yorke peninsulas, with Middleton the familiar Fleurieu training strip when lows track well and banks stay groomed. Kangaroo Island adds heavier reef and beach options for those who commit to the ferry and extra logistics. Wetsuits are year round insurance, and many days trade tropical blue for grey skies, strong rips, and grateful empty peaks.

name: Tasmania
description: The Roaring Forties deliver some of the country's most serious reef and point waves, with Shipstern Bluff standing as the heavy water benchmark when the right swell and crew align. South of Hobart and along the east coast corners, shorter period wind swell still offers everyday sessions for locals in thick rubber. Isolation, cold water, and shifting Southern Ocean weather reward self sufficient surfers more than guidebook tourists.

name: Victoria
description: Bells Beach and Winkipop anchor the state's identity in long, powerful Southern Ocean walls, complete with Easter contest history that helped define modern competitive surfing. Phillip Island and the Mornington Peninsula add more setups within a few hours of Melbourne, where urban crowds drain to the coast whenever a strong cold front approaches. Wetsuits, rips, and Victorian wind are constants beneath the postcard points.

name: Western Australia
description: Indian Ocean groundswell marches thousands of kilometres before unloading on Margaret River's reefs and the southwest's deep water bombies, a region that shaped competitors like Taj Burrow and still hosts CT events. Perth metro and the mid coast offer more user friendly peaks when the southwest monsters stay west. Sharks, long drives, and serious hold downs are part of the deal when the charts turn purple.

name: Wreck Bay Aboriginal Land
description: Jointly managed Booderee country wraps Jervis Bay's south headland, where Cave Beach and nearby Bherwerre setups turn southeast energy into punchy beach and reef peaks when wind cooperates. Camping bookings, park fees, and Aboriginal community protocols matter as much as tide charts, because this is living country, not a theme park. Expect kangaroos on the track, clear water, and a quieter lineup than Sydney, until a long weekend fills the campground.

name: Ngatangiia
description: Muri's lagoon looks tame, but the reef pass at Avana bends swell into a playful left and a longer right off the channel mouth when the period and wind line up. The site carries deep voyaging history, so parking, picnics, and paddle outs stay respectful of locals who treat the water as taonga rather than a stadium. Booties help on the inside, and easterly trades can ruin the face by mid morning.

name: Nikao
description: Black Rock and the Socials peak off the airport fringe reef, bending trade swell into fast pockets that attract one of the island’s busiest lineups when a north pulse runs. It is advanced coral surfing with urchins and photographers on the rocks, not a learner bay. Dawn and a high tide cushion can make the difference between makeable walls and dry reef.

name: Pue
description: Northeast trades wrap into Matavera’s Norrie Park right, a consistent reef wall over bright coral when southeast groundswell fills in. The wreck name on the charts is a reminder to watch the inside on falling tides. Quieter than the airport side, but still a short scooter ride from Avarua when the charts turn green.

name: Rarotonga
description: One road rings the volcano, so every swell window becomes a scooter mission between reef passes like Rutaki and Avaavaroa and the airport side bombs. November through March northern energy is the main season, while trades can blow the east coast out by late morning. Reef booties, a repair kit, and cash for boats matter more than a thick quiver on an island this small.

name: Central
description: Pacific Harbour and the Beqa seaway put you within boat range of Frigates, a long, hollow left that rivals any postcard wave in the country when southwest groundswell meets light trades. It is a fuel burn and time commitment from shore, with resort boats and independent skippers both running when the buoys jump. Crowds ebb with weather, but the reef stays shallow and serious regardless of who is in the channel.

name: Eastern
description: Kadavu’s south coast stares straight into the Southern Ocean, where heavy reef passes like King Kong turn long period energy into wide, technical lefts for crews who accept boat logistics and village protocols. Trades blow hard many afternoons, so dawn and tide strategy separate fun from chop. This is advanced water: sharp coral, long swims, and far fewer charters than the Mamanuca circuit.

name: Northern
description: Vanua Levu and Taveuni anchor the country’s northern surf frontier, with Maqai style reef setups offering rights and lefts across channels that many travelers never bother to reach. Swell can be year round, yet wind is the real filter, and inter island ferries dictate the calendar as much as the forecast. Expect jungle backdrops, thin crowds when you earn them, and booties after every session.

name: Western
description: The Mamanucas are the reason plane loads of surfers connect through Nadi, because Cloudbreak stacks long, thick lefts over shallow reef when southwest groundswell couples with southeast trades. Boat access from Namotu, Tavarua, and nearby charters is the only practical game, and the lineup mixes world tour pedigree with Fijian locals who know every boil on the flat. Nearby Restaurant Left and companion reefs sit in the same channel neighborhood, so etiquette and patience matter as much as courage when the sets stand up.

name: Afaahiti
description: The Taravao isthmus is the doorway to Tahiti Iti, funneling swell toward reef passes like Maraa where a grinding left can run on the right south swell and offshore breeze. It is rural compared with Papeete, with fewer services and more cows on the road than surf shops. Sharp reef, sharks, and shifting wind keep it honest even when the photos look idyllic.

name: Leeward Islands
description: Huahine, Raiatea, Tahaa, and Bora Bora trade deep South Pacific groundswell for lagoon geometry, turning reef passes into playful walls that rarely match Tahiti Iti for heaviness but shine for crystal water and boat access. Pass names change with the charts, and many setups need a willing captain more than a rental car. Cyclone season demands respect, yet dry season south swells still light up the outer reefs without the Teahupo'o circus.

name: Maraa
description: Exposed reef off the Tahiti Nui coast throws a left that can wall up for hundreds of metres when southerly energy meets an east offshore window. Passe de Maraa nearby adds a channel peak that spreads the crowd on good days. Urchins, rips, and passing storms are part of the everyday calculation between glassy mornings and blown trades.

name: Pahiti
description: Shallow lagoon motus off Huahine frame reef passes that peel on the right swell angle, with Fare side channels offering more approachable faces than the Tahiti slabs hundreds of kilometres east. Surf tourism here runs quieter, built around pensions and small boats rather than contest scaffolding. Reef boots, sun cover, and patience for fickle wind days beat showing up with one oversized gun.

name: Paraoro
description: Northwest Tahiti Nui picks up north and northeast energy on points like Orofara when winter lows track north of the island chain, giving punchy reef rides minutes from Papeete traffic. It is not the same south swell machine as the big name end of the island, which means fewer headline days but also fewer boats in the channel. Mornings before the trades and careful tide choice keep sessions makeable over sharp coral.

name: Vairao
description: Vairao’s harbour and Passe de Vairao offer boat first access to Tahiti Iti’s reef landscape, including a workable left on the pass when swell and tide cooperate. From here the road threads toward Teahupo'o minutes away, where channel boats stack on the biggest south swells. Respect village pace, limited parking, and local operators who cap numbers when the reef turns lethal.

name: Îles du Vent
description: Tahiti and Moorea define the Windward chain, yet global surf imagination fixes on Teahupo'o, the shallow slab that has hosted championship tours and Kelly Slater era moments that rewrote what paddle surfing could look like in heavy water. Moorea’s passes add mellower reef options when Tahiti Iti is maxing or blown. South swell season brings the juice, but boats, growing spectator fleets, and razor reef mean this is expert water even when the photos look perfect.

name: San Lazarus archipelago
description: Reef passes around this Mariana chain turn typhoon and trade swell into short, punchy walls, with spots near Talofofo Bay and the east side lighting up fastest when wind eases. Warm water and military island logistics keep the scene small but committed, and shallow coral means every wipeout has consequences.

name: State of Pohnpei
description: Outer reef and channel setups around Pohnpei wake up on long period north and east swell, with Palikir Pass and nearby reefs offering clean walls when trades back off. You trade consistency for very low crowds, humid weather, and boat logistics that can cancel a session before it starts.

name: South Province
description: Barrier reef passes from Noumea southward can produce long, groomed reef rides when Southern Ocean swell threads into the lagoon openings, with Dumbea Pass the classic benchmark on the right day. It is world class but tide dependent, and wind plus boat access costs often decide whether you surf or just watch perfect water from shore.

name: Auckland
description: Black sand west coast beaches pick up Tasman pulses within easy reach of the city, with Piha and Muriwai the default call for heavy beachbreak sessions. Crowds, rips, and fast weather swings are the trade for being close to New Zealand's biggest airport and board shops.

name: Marlborough
description: Cook Strait winds and long travel distances shape this coast more than social media, with Marfells and exposed bays offering fickle but clean walls when storm tracks line up. It is a score or nothing region where road time, tide timing, and patience matter more than daily consistency.

name: Nelson
description: Northern South Island corners can hold fun wind swell and occasional groundswell windows, with Wharariki and west facing beaches the better bets when fronts move through. The payoff is space and scenery, while the downside is short windows and constant wind management.

name: North Island
description: Two very different coasts make this island a year round mission, from Raglan's long left points to Gisborne's east coast beachbreak and reef mix. It is New Zealand's busiest surf map, so the best days bring crowds, but there are enough options to keep moving when wind changes.

name: Northland
description: Far north reefs and long beachbreaks receive swell from multiple angles, with Ahipara and Shipwreck Bay delivering long left walls in the right wind. Distances are bigger than they look on a map, and once you are up here you commit to sparse services and rapidly changing weather.

name: South Island
description: Southern Ocean energy, alpine weather, and long coastlines create everything from mellow town beachbreaks to heavy cold water reefs, with St Clair and Sumner as familiar urban anchors. The scale is huge, so scoring often means driving between systems rather than waiting at one break.

name: Southland
description: Raw southern exposure and colder water define this region, with Colac Bay the local longboard left and nearby points turning on when west swell wraps cleanly. Sessions are often windy and lonely, and that isolation is exactly why the lineup stays thin.

name: Taranaki
description: A perfectly placed volcanic coast turns Tasman swell into one of the country's most reliable circuits, with Fitzroy and Stent Road as core options in different moods. It is famously consistent, but black sand rips and crowd pressure on good days keep everyone honest.

name: Tasman
description: Most coast here is better known for wind and paddling, but exposed beaches near Farewell Spit and Wharariki can offer quality peaks in the right storm track. You accept lower hit rate than Taranaki in exchange for emptier lineups and dramatic, remote coast.

name: Waikato
description: Long left walls around Raglan are the headline, with Manu Bay still the point everyone measures themselves against when it is running. West coast consistency is high, yet crowd intensity and long paddle outs are the real tax on every good forecast.

name: Wellington
description: Harbor geography and Cook Strait wind make this a tricky but rewarding coast, with Lyall Bay and Titahi Bay offering sessions when the angle and tide align. Forecasts can flip quickly, so locals chase short windows and stay flexible rather than waiting for all day perfection.

name: West Coast
description: Open Tasman exposure means regular swell and regular weather, with Westport and Greymouth the familiar hubs for punchy beachbreak surfing. Water is cold and conditions can turn fast, but crowd levels stay low compared with the North Island.

name: State of Airai
description: Rock Islands channels and nearby reef ledges can produce short, rippable walls when east swell arrives and wind settles. Access is mostly by boat and local knowledge, so even good conditions can stay quiet compared with better known Pacific surf zones.

name: State of Melekeok
description: This coast sees less traffic than Koror side channels, but outer reef sections and passes can line up on clean northeast energy with almost no one around. Sessions depend on boat timing, tide windows, and respecting marine protected areas.

name: State of Ngeremlengui
description: Mangrove backed waterways hide access routes to exposed reef passes that wake up on north and east swell, giving short, technical rides over sharp coral. It is a planning region more than a paddle out and see region, and missed tides usually end the day.

name: East Sepik Province
description: River mouths and reef sections along this coast can turn cyclone and trade swell into quality but inconsistent peaks, especially near Wewak-facing stretches. Logistics, safety planning, and limited surf infrastructure matter as much as wave quality in this part of PNG.

name: New Ireland
description: Fringing reefs and remote channels around Kavieng have produced some of the Pacific's longest barrels when season and wind align, with Nusa and nearby reefs the classic call. It is high reward surfing with boats, tropical storms, and limited backup options if gear fails.

name: Atua
description: Southeast Upolu catches south swell that wraps into reef passes and rivermouth mouths, with Salani side setups providing some of the more dependable options in this part of Samoa. Village access, tides, and coral depth are the daily tradeoffs even when conditions look friendly from shore.

name: Fusi
description: South coast reefs in this area can turn short period energy into peaky, workable walls for surfers willing to watch tide carefully and avoid exposed coral heads. Sessions are often uncrowded, but weather squalls and road access can change plans quickly.

name: Gagaifomauga
description: North coast Savai'i offers cleaner trades at times and reef breaks that can run longer than expected when the swell angle is right. It is less developed than Upolu's resort side, so you trade comfort for space and local pace.

name: Gaga‘emauga
description: Inner bays and outer reefs here are highly tide sensitive, with brief windows where otherwise heavy sections become makeable. The upside is low crowd pressure, while the downside is long waits between truly lined up days.

name: Lotofagā
description: South shore Upolu reefs near this coastline can produce hollow sections on stronger south swells, especially early before trades build. Coral entries and village land access keep the scene respectful and small.

name: Luatuanu‘u
description: Northeast exposures receive mixed swell directions, creating shorter rides that can still be fun when winds stay light. It is more of a local mission zone than a destination circuit, with tide and reef depth controlling everything.

name: Matavai
description: Northwest Savai'i waters can hold playful reef peaks on modest swell days, with cleaner conditions often tied to morning wind lulls. Services are limited, so surfers usually plan around fuel, food, and daylight rather than chasing late sessions.

name: Palauli
description: Southwest Savai'i has several reef corners that wake up under bigger south pulses, offering faster, hollower lines than much of Upolu. It remains lightly surfed due to distance and setup demands, which is both the draw and the challenge.

name: Utumalama Point
description: This exposed headland area can focus swell into punchy peaks when winds back off, but the usable window is usually short and tide controlled. Locals who know reef exits score most often here.

name: Vaisigano
description: Close to Apia but still dependent on swell angle, these reefs and points can offer quick sessions before work when conditions line up. Urban access helps, though crowd and water quality after heavy rain can become real tradeoffs.

name: Va‘a-o-Fonoti
description: Rugged east Upolu coast catches open ocean energy with fewer built up beaches, producing raw reef sessions when south and east swell combine. It is beautiful and undercrowded, but wind, current, and coral make it unsuitable for casual paddles.

name: Tongatapu
description: Fringing reefs around the capital island pick up south and east swell enough to deliver fun, warm water sessions, with Ha'atafu and nearby reefs as the common references. Consistency is moderate, and tides plus coral depth decide whether the day is playful or punishing.

name: Buenos Aires
description: Long Atlantic beachbreak stretches from Mar del Plata down the coast, with Playa Grande and Miramar producing everything from fun ramps to heavy winter closeouts. It is Argentina's most active surf belt, but cold water, strong wind, and crowded summer city beaches are the constant tradeoff.

name: Rio Negro
description: Patagonian wind and open Atlantic exposure create raw, powerful beachbreak sessions around El Condor and Playas Doradas when swell and weather finally align. Distances are huge and services sparse, so this is more expedition surfing than daily check before work.

name: Alagoas
description: Warm northeast coast water and reef ledges can produce short, punchy waves near Maragogi and Praia do Francês when wind settles. Most days are playful rather than heavy, with tides and wind direction deciding whether it is worth paddling.

name: Bahia
description: Long tropical coastline mixes point and beach setups, with Itacare and Stella Maris standing out when south swell and local wind cooperate. Carnival season energy and city growth bring crowds, but the variety of breaks keeps Bahia on every Brazilian surf map.

name: Ceará
description: Trade swell and wind shape this coast almost year round, with Jericoacoara and Taiba offering rippable peaks when the direction is right. Water stays warm and sessions are frequent, but side winds and shifting sandbanks can turn quality quickly.

name: Espírito Santo
description: Exposed points and beachbreaks between Vitoria and Guarapari can turn south pulses into clean walls, with Camburi and Setiba often leading local call lists. It sits between the heavier Rio and Bahia scenes, giving a solid middle ground with less hype but regular surf.

name: Maranhão
description: North coast wind and river influence make this a lower hit rate surf region, though stretches near Sao Marcos Bay and Atins can become rideable on stronger swell events. It is more of a score when it happens coastline than a daily destination.

name: Paraná
description: Southern beachbreak coast can fire under long period south swell, with Matinhos and Ilha do Mel offering cleaner peaks when winds stay light. Winter fronts bring the better power, but colder water and fast weather changes require flexibility.

name: Paraíba
description: Compact coast near Joao Pessoa picks up short period swell with reef and beach options, with Intermares and Cabedelo the best known calls. It is friendly in warm water terms, but consistency is lower than Rio Grande do Norte just to the north.

name: Pará
description: Huge estuary and river systems limit classic surf consistency, but exposed ocean pockets near Salinopolis and Mosqueiro can produce workable peaks during stronger Atlantic pulses. Travel logistics and tides dominate planning more than contest style forecasting.

name: Pernambuco
description: Recife area reefs and beaches hold a historic scene, with Boa Viagem and Maracaipe often discussed for very different reasons: quality walls on one side and shark risk management on the other. Timing tide and choosing spots carefully is mandatory here, not optional.

name: Rio de Janeiro
description: World Tour history and urban beach culture collide here, with Saquarema and Arpoador as headline references from elite heats to dawn patrol locals. The state offers year round options, but crowds, traffic, and shifting sandbars mean scoring still takes work.

name: Rio Grande do Norte
description: Consistent northeast swell keeps this state active, with Ponta Negra and Baia Formosa producing quality surf and helping launch world champion Italo Ferreira from this coast. Warm water and frequent sessions are the draw, while wind and weekend crowds are the tax.

name: Rio Grande do Sul
description: Cold fronts and long Atlantic beaches shape a gritty surf culture around Torres and Tramandai, where strong south swell can deliver heavy, windy sessions. It is less tropical postcard and more neoprene and persistence, especially in winter.

name: Santa Catarina
description: South swells and varied coastline make this one of the country's most dependable regions, with Praia Mole and Silveira regularly delivering quality walls. Water is cooler than the northeast and weather can turn quickly, but consistency keeps surfers moving here year round.

name: Sergipe
description: Short coastline still finds surf windows around Atalaia and nearby sandbars when east and southeast swell align. It is a smaller scene with fewer options, so wind and tide timing matter more than chasing named marquee breaks.

name: São Paulo
description: State depth and wave variety are why so many pros emerged here, with Maresias and Ubatuba central to the culture and to Gabriel Medina's rise. Cold fronts can light up world class conditions, but dense populations mean crowded peaks are part of daily reality.

name: Antofagasta
description: Desert headlands and deepwater exposure create powerful lefts and rights near Antofagasta city when south swell pulses into the coast. Water is cooler and conditions often windy, so the best sessions belong to surfers who time dawn and tide precisely.

name: Atacama
description: Remote mining coast hides quality point and beach setups around Caldera and Bahia Inglesa on the right storm track. Flat spells can be long, but when Pacific energy arrives the lineups stay far lighter than central Chile.

name: Los Lagos Region
description: Rain, rivers, and island channels shape this southern zone, with Ancud and Maullin areas offering cold, powerful sessions under Southern Ocean weather. Forecasting is harder than central Chile, yet crowd pressure is far lower for those willing to travel.

name: Los Ríos Region
description: Rocky points and beachbreaks near Valdivia can turn on in solid south swells, with Niebla and Mehuin as common regional references. It is a high quality but cold and weather sensitive scene where short windows are normal.

name: Maule
description: Long beaches near Constitucion and Curanipe absorb frequent Pacific energy, producing heavy, wind affected peaks that reward tide timing. It is a working coast first and surf destination second, which helps keep crowds manageable.

name: Región de Arica y Parinacota
description: Northern Chile's border coast houses one of the country's heaviest barrels, with El Gringo in Arica setting the standard for advanced reef surfing. Warmer water than central Chile is the bonus, but local knowledge and shallow reef are non negotiable.

name: Región de Coquimbo
description: Long points and beachbreaks from La Serena southward offer regular surf windows, with Pichidangui and nearby reefs working best under clean south swell lines. It is less crowded than Santiago's immediate coast yet still close enough for weekend pressure.

name: Región de Valparaíso
description: Close to the capital and packed with options, this coast runs from urban Reñaca peaks to wind exposed Ritoque beachbreak. Accessibility is excellent, but so are crowds, and weekend traffic can cost more time than the session itself.

name: Región del Biobío
description: Concepcion area beaches and points can handle significant south swell, with Dichato and nearby open coast setups producing punchy, powerful sessions. Wind and cold water are constants, but consistency is strong through winter cycles.

name: Región del Libertador General Bernardo O’Higgins
description: Punta de Lobos defines this region, serving one of South America's most iconic long left walls when winter swell hits. Pichilemu town infrastructure makes access easy, yet crowd intensity and raw power keep the lineup serious.

name: Tarapacá
description: Iquique's urban coast and nearby points pick up north and south energy in different seasons, with Cavancha and outer reefs offering occasional quality windows. Desert climate keeps water clear and weather dry, but consistency still depends on swell direction.

name: Atlántico
description: Trade swell gives this coast frequent small to medium beachbreak days near Puerto Colombia and Salgar, especially in windy season. It is accessible from Barranquilla, but quality is often short period and tide sensitive.

name: Departamento de Bolívar
description: Cartagena side beaches are better known for travel than high performance surf, though exposed corners can produce rideable windswell at the right time. Heat and crowds are guaranteed, while true quality days are selective.

name: Departamento de Córdoba
description: Caribbean beach stretches around Moñitos and nearby towns can offer playful peaks on stronger trade pulses. Most sessions are mellow and seasonal, with limited surf infrastructure compared with Pacific Colombia.

name: Departamento de La Guajira
description: Northernmost Caribbean desert coast receives wind and swell that can create clean, uncrowded lines near Palomino and Cabo de la Vela. Logistics are harder than map distance suggests, so surfers need transport planning and local guidance.

name: Departamento del Chocó
description: Rainforest Pacific coast delivers Colombia's most consistent and powerful surf, with Nuqui and El Valle as the usual gateways to quality beachbreak and reef sessions. Boat access, rain, and remoteness keep crowds low but planning demands high.

name: Departamento del Magdalena
description: Santa Marta side points and beaches can be fun during winter trade swell windows, with Mendihuaca and nearby stretches attracting local crews. Water is warm and scenery is huge, but consistency and size are modest most of the year.

name: Provincia de Esmeraldas
description: Warm northern Ecuador coast can be surprisingly consistent, with Mompiche and Atacames offering everything from long softer walls to punchier sections on bigger south pulses. Access is straightforward, but rain season and river outflow can quickly change water quality and shape.

name: Provincia de Galápagos
description: Volcanic island points and reef edges wake up on long period south swells, with Punta Carola and Tongo Reef as the best known references for visiting surfers. It is a world class setting but heavily regulated and expensive to reach, so surf windows must be planned around park rules and boats.

name: Provincia de Manabí
description: Central coast variety keeps this province active, with Canoa and Manta side beaches producing frequent sessions across different swell directions. It is one of Ecuador's most dependable belts, though crowd spikes and afternoon wind can quickly degrade quality.

name: Provincia de Santa Elena
description: Point and beach setups around Montanita and Olon are the country's best known user friendly waves, with enough consistency to support a year round surf town scene. Popularity brings crowd pressure and nightlife noise, so dawn patrol often beats sunset chaos.

name: Provincia del Guayas
description: Most coastline here is better known for ports and estuaries, but Playas and nearby exposed beaches can provide rideable windswell and occasional groundswell windows. It is a lower consistency option where timing and local reports matter more than reputation.

name: Ancash
description: Cold Humboldt influence and broad desert bays create punchy sessions around Tortugas and Tuquillo when south swell arrives. It is less famous than northern Peru, but clean uncrowded days reward surfers who can handle cooler water and sparse infrastructure.

name: Arequipa
description: Long southern points and beachbreaks can turn on under winter south pulses, with Camana and Punta de Bombon as common regional references. Wind and distance keep crowds low, but consistency is moderate and road planning is essential.

name: Ica
description: Desert headlands and long beaches near Paracas and Puerto Caballas offer quality on the right swell angle, often with strong currents and cooler water. It is a score based coast where conditions can look perfect one tide and close out the next.

name: La Libertad
description: Home to one of surfing's legendary lefts, Chicama can run for remarkable distances when long period south swell lines up, while Huanchaco keeps daily culture and caballito history alive. Crowds are part of the package now, but the wave quality still justifies the hype.

name: Lambayeque
description: North coast beachbreak around Pimentel and Puerto Eten provides warm water sessions and workable peaks on mixed swell. It is less reliable than Piura but easier to access for quick missions from inland cities.

name: Lima region
